t: #2539 — Count the Number of Good Subsequences
o: A good subsequence is non-empty and every character that appears in it appears the same number of times L. We count labeled subsequences (by index sets), modulo 1e9+7. For "abcd" every non-empty subset qualifies (15). For "aabb", the bad ones are the empty set, the two "aab" index sets and the two "abb" index sets, leaving 11. With n up to 1e4 we can precompute factorials and group characters by frequency.
k: Group a good subsequence by its common frequency L: each character contributes either exactly L copies or none.
For a fixed L, the number of ways is the product over characters of (C(f_c, L) + 1); subtracting 1 removes the all-empty selection.
Each good subsequence has a unique L (its common frequency), so summing over L counts everything exactly once.

a.i: Let f_c be the frequency of character c. For each L from 1 to max frequency, the number of index subsets where every used character appears exactly L times is Π_c (C(f_c, L) + 1). This product counts the empty selection once per L, so subtract 1 each time and sum over L.
s: Count character frequencies and precompute factorials/inverse factorials up to n.
For each L = 1..maxFreq compute the product of (C(f_c, L) + 1) over all characters.
Add product − 1 to the answer for each L.
a.t: O(n + 26·F) where F is the maximum character frequency — factorial tables are linear and the double loop is bounded by 26·n.
a.sp: O(n) for the factorial and inverse factorial tables.

w: The key leap is realizing each good subsequence corresponds to exactly one common frequency L, which turns a potentially exponential enumeration into a product formula. Common mistakes: forgetting to subtract the empty selection per L, or trying to subtract 'bad' subsequences from 2^n (which double-counts). A follow-up might ask for the count of good *distinct* strings, which needs a different (DP on distinct subsequence) technique.
